extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims are directed to an 'abstract idea' (and thus patent-ineligible) under §101, with categories, tests, and examples for examiner use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to fundamental economic practices (e.g., hedging risk, managing insurance, intermediated settlement, price optimization) are examples of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains that the Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have identified hedging, insurance-related management, and other financial or business practices as "fundamental economic practice" abstract ideas (citing Bilski, Bancorp, Alice, etc.). Examples listed include: mitigating settlement risk; rules for conducting a wagering game; financial instruments designed to protect against investment risk; offer-based price optimization; local processing of payments for remotely purchased goods; using an external marking on mail to communicate sender/recipient/contents; placing an order based on displayed market information. The guidance highlights that claims which attempt to "patent the use of the abstract idea ... and then instruct the use of well-known [calculations]" can be directed to an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting commercial or legal interactions—agreements (contracts), legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities/behaviors, and business relations—may be directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: buySAFE (transaction performance guaranty/contractual relationship), Bancorp (stable value protected life insurance policy calculations), Accenture v. Guidewire (processing insurance claims under a policy), Fort Properties (aggregating real property and master agreements for tax-free exchanges), Ultramercial (displaying ads in exchange for access), structuring a sales force or marketing company, algorithms for business visit scheduling, offer-based price optimization, database/system for processing credit applications and creating financing packages (Credit Acceptance), clearing-house processing of credit applications (Dealertrack). The guidance emphasizes that contractual relationships or legal obligations implemented in claims have been characterized as abstract ideas when they are essentially business or legal concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite managing personal behavior, relationships, social activities, teaching, or following rules/instructions are candidates for being abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include storing user-selected spending limits and notifying users when limits are reached (budgeting - Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One), filtering content, considering historical usage information when inputting data, methods a neurologist follows (mental processes), voting processes (Voter Verified), providing information without interfering with a person's primary activity (Interval Licensing - attention management), and rules for playing games (In re Marco Guldenaar - dice game wagering). The guidance notes such activities are "methods of organizing human activity" and align with prior abstract-idea holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper, are "mental processes" and thus are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance cites case law (CyberSource, Benson, Mayo, Parker v. Flook) and explains mental processes include observations, evaluations, judgments, and opinions. It clarifies that the term refers to a type of abstract idea rather than the statutory claim category, and that both product and process claims can recite mental processes (e.g., computer systems or media claims can nonetheless be mental-process-type abstract ideas). Examiners are instructed that methods which can be performed mentally or with simple physical aids are unpatentable abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point A: If a claim includes limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind, it is not a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims do not recite mental processes when they include limitations that humans cannot practically perform mentally (e.g., specialized technical steps that exceed human capability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited examples where claims were not mental processes: detecting suspicious activity using network monitors and analyzing network packets (SRI Int’l v. Cisco); GPS calculations for absolute position/time involving pseudoranges (SiRF Tech.); specific multi-step data encryption methods (Synopsys); rendering halftone images pixel-by-pixel by comparing to a blue noise mask (Research Corp. Techs.). Examiners should recognize when claimed steps require technical processing or apparatus beyond mental performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point B: Claims that encompass a human performing the steps mentally (with or without a physical aid) recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim reads on a human performing the claimed steps mentally, or mentally with a simple physical aid (pen and paper, slide rule), the claim falls within the mental processes group and thus is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance explains that use of a physical aid does not negate the mental nature of the limitation; it merely accounts for memory/capacity variation. Cited authorities include Benson, Synopsys, CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card numbers could be done by writing a list), Flook (computations by pencil and paper), University of Florida Research Foundation v. GE (specification describing flowsheets/patient charts), and Symantec (screening messages could be performed by a human). Examiners should consider whether claim language "reads on" a person performing the steps mentally or with simple aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point C: Claims that require a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can recite a mental process even if the claim is framed as being performed on a computer; implementation on generic computer hardware does not automatically make it non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance cites Benson (algorithm carried out in existing computers is still an abstract idea) and Mortgage Grader (concept could be performed by humans without a computer). Examiners are instructed to consider the broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the specification to determine whether the claimed invention is merely a concept that can be performed mentally and is simply claimed as performed on a generic computer, in a computer environment, or using a computer as a tool. If so, treat it as reciting a mental process/abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on reviewing the specification for computer-implemented claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating computer-implemented claims for mental-process abstract ideas, examiners should review the specification to determine whether the applicant describes the concept as performed in the human mind or merely claims it on generic computer hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should look for specification language that shows the claimed invention is described as a human-concept (e.g., cognitive actions) merely implemented on a computer. If the specification indicates the invention is essentially a mental process performed using generic computing, that supports treating the claim as an abstract idea. The guidance also notes examiners should consider whether the computer is performing functions that cannot practically be done mentally (see Point A) versus merely being a tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoint 1: Performing a mental process on a generic computer is an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed steps are mental/cognitive actions that have historically been performed by humans, performing them on a generic computer does not remove their abstract nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Voter Verified (voting, verifying, submitting votes are "human cognitive actions" performed for hundreds of years but claimed on a computer) and Versata (pricing determination implemented on general purpose computer hardware). The guidance reiterates that claiming longstanding human activities on generic computers supports a finding of an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes can appear in product claims as well as process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The categorization of 'mental processes' applies to the type of abstract idea recited and is not limited to process claims; product (e.g., system, computer-readable media) claims can also recite mental-process-type abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance cites Versata as an example where product claims (computer systems, computer-readable media) were identified as reciting mental-process-type abstract ideas. Examiners should therefore apply the mental-process analysis across claim categories.
